question: Six Member States, including Slovakia, reject the proposal for a further significant reduction in free emission allowances for industrial enterprises. They warn that this measure risks causing a massive shift of production outside the EU (carbon leakage) loss of competitiveness and the deindustrialisation of Europe. In light of the foregoing: 1.

What serious negative economic impacts does the Commission expect following a significant reduction in the volume of free emission allowances, in particular in terms of rising energy prices, loss of competitiveness and a decline in investment in energyintensive sectors?

Has the Commission assessed the real risk of plant closures and the relocation of production to third countries with lower environmental standards, and what are its estimates of the scale of this carbon leakage?

What specific and effective measures does the Commission plan to introduce to protect European industry, in order to prevent further deindustrialisation and the massive relocation of jobs outside the Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) Under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), free allocation supports competitiveness during the transition while maintaining incentives to cut emissions and rewarding efficiency rather than simply subsidising emissions. On 17 July 2026 the Commission adopted a proposal to review the ETS1.

Accompanying this proposal is a Staff Working Document2, which includes an evaluation of the functioning of the ETS and an impact assessment3 of different policy options for the future. These assessments have concluded that, so far, the carbon leakage protection has been effective and that the reforms introduced continue to reduce carbon leakage risks and improve the competitiveness of European industry.

Conscious that a reduction in free emissions allowances can create short-term pressure on energy-intensive, carbon-leakage exposed sectors, the review includes other carbon leakage prevention measures as well as a significant increase in the support for investments in the decarbonisation of the EU, in particular through the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank and the Investment Booster.

Furthermore, the Commission is taking multiple measures to support industry in the current energy crisis affecting supply of imported fossil fuels, including under the Affordable Energy Action Plan, AccelerateEU4 and the Electrification Action Plan5.
